name: Kramer's Rotating Perfect Fluid
description: A bounded perfect fluid in rigid rotation, with negative pressure and positive energy density.
convention: We use the standard Ricci contraction, $R_{\mu\nu}=R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$, and Euler's number $e$ as the base of natural logarithms.
history: Pressure is negative throughout the rotating body Dietrich Kramer found in 1984 [kramer1984fluid, chinea1999kramer]. It reaches its lowest value at the centre and rises to zero on a closed surface. The energy density remains positive and exceeds the magnitude of the pressure throughout the fluid [chinea1999kramer].¶The equation of state fixes $\varepsilon+3p$ at a positive constant, where $\varepsilon$ is the energy density and $p$ the pressure [chinea1999kramer]. The fluid rotates rigidly about a regular axis. Two commuting symmetries express stationarity and axial symmetry, and reflection across the equatorial plane exchanges the two hemispheres. The distance from the centre to a pole is shorter than the distance from the centre to the equator [chinea1999kramer].¶The parameter $m>0$ sets the length scale through the factor $1/(2m)$ in the line element [chinea1999kramer]. The rotation parameter $b$ must exceed $2e$ for a nonempty fluid body, where $e$ is the base of natural logarithms. At the centre, the vorticity has magnitude $(b+e)\sqrt{m/(2be)}$ and remains nonzero throughout this family [chinea1999kramer].¶Francisco Javier Chinea Trujillo and María Jesús Pareja García examined the geometry of this body in 1999 [chinea1999kramer]. They found that, for sufficiently large values of $b$, the surface of zero pressure has negative Gaussian curvature near the equator within a surface of constant time. The circumference of its latitude circles then reaches a maximum between each pole and the equator. At the limiting value $b\simeq8.603$, the equatorial circumference shrinks to zero and the Gaussian curvature there diverges [chinea1999kramer].¶Within the spatial geometry at constant time, the shortest distance from the boundary to the rotation axis increases from pole to equator [chinea1999kramer]. The distance from the centre to the boundary has a local maximum at the equator. Meridional geodesics that cross the equatorial plane at right angles stay within the body between their two boundary intersections [chinea1999kramer].

coordinates.name: Published Radial Coordinate
domains: \eta=1\;\text{(regular rotation axis, where the polar chart fails)}

parameters.description: A positive inverse squared length, with length scale $\ell=1/\sqrt{2m}$

A dimensionless rotation parameter, $2e<b<b_\star$, where $b_\star=(\eta_\star+1)e^{\eta_\star}\simeq8.603$ and $\eta_\star>1$ is the nontrivial root of $(\eta_\star+1)(2e^{\eta_\star-1}-e^{2\eta_\star-2})=2$
A dimensionless exponential of the radial coordinate

A dimensionless function; the pressure $p=m(1+\eta-F)/(2\kappa_0)$ and energy density $\varepsilon=m(1-3\eta+3F)/(2\kappa_0)$ obey $\varepsilon+3p=2m/\kappa_0$, with $\kappa_0=8\pi G/c^4$ the Einstein coupling
The equatorial surface radius, defined by $(\eta_e+1)e^{\eta_e}=b$

coordinates.convention: We use dimensionless coordinates $(\tau,\eta,\xi,\phi)$, with $\tau$ along the fluid world lines and $\phi$ the azimuth. The radial coordinate is $\eta$, and the latitude is $\xi$. Components use these coordinates directly, with no rescaling by $c$; a dot denotes differentiation with respect to an affine parameter, and dimensional time is $T=\ell\tau/c$.

related.text: Rigid rotation with the same linear equation of state, $\varepsilon+3p=\mathrm{constant}$. The two fluids belong to the stationary axisymmetric family of algebraic type D [racz1996fluid].
Spherical fluid equilibrium with pressure balancing gravity. Kramer's body has rigid rotation and negative pressure within a closed surface [chinea1999kramer].
The exterior field of a slowly rotating body, through second order in its angular velocity. Kramer's exact fluid has finite rotation throughout its bounded family [chinea1999kramer].
